The questions then become confused, the metaphors impenetrable, and the issue of who is the criminal, who the prisoner and who the observed becomes convoluted beyond resolution or care.
But although philosophically provocative, a man spending two decades on a barren plain is dramatically inert.
Sad to say, this thin and philosophically opaque work is pretty deadly too.
The surrealism feels lazy and the humour is unsatisfying.

Brook's flinty text, co-written with his collaborator Marie-Hélène Estienne, is so inexpressive its almost inert and there's so little action or panche that, at times, it feels as if the theatre's fallen out.
The British master-director settles for vaguely Beckett-inflected bafflement.

Despite its minimalist, philosophical flavour, The Prisoner smacks of narcissism: a play by a great absentee master of the British stage we can go and see and feel we have been in the presence of 'high' art. Missable.

Brook and Estienne's exploration of justice seems to be a half-baked melting pot, full of interesting snapshots, but results in a piece that, despite its swift 70-minute running time, lingers a little too long on the surface without digging deeper.
This play is beautifully acted and holds concentration on and in every moment.
The Prisoner is self-indulgent and lacks the skill to convince the audience to be equally obsessed by its moral thrashing.
The Prisoner is full of potential and raises many profound questions.

cn.t: Peter Brook's minimalist meditation on guilt and forgiveness falls frustratingly flat, with critics finding it pretentious, opaque, and dramatically inert despite occasional praise for its acting.
